An arrangement is a set of decisions about who plays what, where, and when they keep
quiet. This series takes the site's backing band apart one player at a time. Each example
below is the band itself: press **▶ Play**, then use the buttons under **Who plays** to
switch players in and out while it runs. Under the buttons, the last four bars the band
played are written out, one staff per player, so you can see what you are hearing.

The four lessons:

1. **Who plays what** (this page): the jobs in a rhythm section and how they stack up.
2. [Bass and drums](arrange-bass-drums.qmd): the foundation, and why the bass follows the kick drum.
3. [Guitar and keyboards](arrange-chords.qmd): comping, register, and two chord players at once.
4. [The organ](arrange-organ.qmd): tonebars, chorus, swell pedal and Leslie, on a model you can play.

## 1. Four jobs

A rhythm section shares out four jobs:

- **Time.** The drums say where the beat is and how it is divided: straight or swung,
  busy or calm. Everyone else leans on them.
- **The bottom.** The bass says which chord this is by playing its root, mostly on the
  strong beats, and it ties the harmony to the drums' rhythm.
- **The harmony and the inner rhythm.** Guitar and keyboards fill the middle: the rest of the
  chord, played in a pattern that sits between the drums' hits.
- **The melody.** A singer or soloist. The rhythm section's job is to leave room for it.

A band sounds good when those jobs don't step on each other. Most of arranging is
deciding who *doesn't* play.

## 2. Build it up one player at a time

Start with only the drums, then add the bass, then the guitar. Listen for what each
player adds. The drums alone have rhythm but no key. The bass adds the chord changes. The
guitar adds the colour of each chord (major or minor) and fills the gaps in the rhythm.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="rock" data-chart="C|Am|F|G" data-tempo="100" data-comp="guitar" data-on="drums"></div>

Now take one away at a time. Without the bass, the band suddenly sounds thin and high.
Without the drums, the guitar and bass have to keep time themselves and they sound
loose. Without the guitar, the bass and drums still hold the song up: that's why they
are called the *foundation*.

## 3. Register: everyone gets a floor of the house

Look at the written parts while the band plays. The bass sits low, under the bass
clef. The guitar sits in the middle. The drums aren't pitched, but the kick is low,
the snare is in the middle and the cymbals are high.

When two players share a register they blur together. The easiest fix is to move one of
them. Here the piano comps in a ballad, then plays the same notes an octave higher, then
an octave lower. Hear how the low one gets in the way of the bass and muddies the
chords, and how the high one leaves the middle empty for a singer.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="pop" data-chart="C|G|Am|F" data-tempo="72" data-comp="piano" data-choice-label="Piano:" data-choices='[{"label":"Where it was written","opts":{"octave":{"comp":0}}},{"label":"An octave up","opts":{"octave":{"comp":1}}},{"label":"An octave down","opts":{"octave":{"comp":-1}}}]'></div>

## 4. Same chords, three bands

A style is a set of these decisions made together. These three play the same four
chords. Switch players off in each to hear how the jobs are shared out differently.

**Rock:** bass on every eighth note, guitar strumming eighths, a backbeat on 2 and 4.
Everyone plays the same grid, so it drives.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="rock" data-chart="C|Am|F|G" data-tempo="112" data-comp="guitar"></div>

**Reggae:** the guitar plays only on the off-beats and the drums leave beat 1 empty.
The bass carries the downbeat by itself. Take the bass out and the beat is gone.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="reggae" data-chart="C|Am|F|G" data-tempo="80" data-comp="guitar"></div>

**Swing:** the bass walks a note on every beat, the ride cymbal plays the swung pattern,
and the piano plays short chords now and then, mostly off the beat. The piano part
changes every time round: in jazz the comping is a conversation, not a fixed pattern.

<div class="ar-demo" data-style="swing" data-chart="Dm7|G7|Cmaj7|A7" data-tempo="132"></div>

## 5. Try it

- In each example, find the one player you could lose with the least damage. That
  player is the first to drop out when a singer comes in.
- Turn on only bass and drums in the reggae example, then only guitar and drums. Which
  pair still sounds like reggae?
